name: Neck liposuction

lead: Neck liposuction, also called submental liposuction, removes fat beneath the chin and along the neck through small incisions. People use it to reduce a double chin and define the jawline and neck, and it is sometimes combined with platysma repair or other lifting techniques.

A suction cannula is passed through small incisions, usually under local tumescent anesthesia in published series. The evidence is mostly surgeon case series, including a 320-case safety series and a 500-procedure study comparing skin retraction by treatment site. On forums, users describe it as a permanent-fat-removal option for a sharper neck-jaw transition.

paras: It is performed by a surgeon, often under local anesthesia, and the fullness reduction shows once swelling settles. It may be done alone or paired with muscle repair or a lift when skin or bands are also a concern.
Published risks include infection, contour irregularities and unfavorable results with poor patient selection. Skin retraction varies by treatment site, and skin laxity affects the final look.

angle.text: Neck liposuction removes fat under the chin and along the neck, reducing a double chin and defining the jawline. The reduction in fullness is visible once swelling settles. Support comes from surgeon case series, including a 320-case safety report.

lead: Neck liposuction, also called submental liposuction or 'double chin lipo', removes fat beneath the chin and along the neck through small incisions using thin suction cannulas. By taking out the fat pad that blurs the line between jaw and neck, it is used to sharpen the cervicomental angle and make the jawline read more clearly, and it is sometimes combined with platysma repair or other lifting techniques.[1][2][3][4]

The procedure draws on the general liposuction techniques developed from the mid-1970s and on tumescent local anesthesia, introduced by dermatologist Jeffrey Klein in the 1980s, which lets the neck be treated with local anesthetic alone.[5] Published evidence consists mostly of surgeon case series and technique papers, including a 35-patient retrospective analysis of neck liposuction with platysma repair,[2] a 320-patient safety series using tumescent anesthesia,[6] a 987-patient complication series,[7] and a 500-procedure study of skin retraction by treatment site.[8]

Online, the procedure is discussed as a permanent-fat-removal option for people whose neck fullness, rather than jaw bone structure, is the thing blurring the jawline. Non-surgical fat-reduction methods such as injectable deoxycholic acid and cryolipolysis are used for the same area and are discussed alongside it.[9][10]

paras: In the procedures described in the literature, tumescent local anesthetic solution is infiltrated into the area, a cannula removes superficial adipose tissue through small incisions, and the overlying skin is redraped.[8][3] Reviews of the technique cover neck and lower-face anatomy, patient selection, tumescent anesthesia, equipment and ancillary steps such as laser lipolysis, fractional CO2 resurfacing and treatment of platysmal bands.[3]

Surgeons describe a spectrum of approaches. One group reported wide undermining of a rhomboid area of skin with a very thin fat layer preserved, under local anesthesia and with a dressing for three days, in 118 patients treated between 2005 and 2012.[11] Others describe an enhancement of neck liposuction results using the FAMI technique,[12] and radiofrequency-assisted liposuction (FaceTite) combined with buccal fat pad excision for facial slimming.[13] A case report describes submental liposuction with the VASER ultrasound system.[14]

Liposuction as a general technique emerged in the late 1960s and 1970s. In Rome, Arpad and Giorgio Fischer developed a blunt cannula connected to suction, first used on the outer thighs; Yves-Gérard Illouz and Fournier extended the method to the whole body, and in the 1980s American dermatologist Jeffrey Klein published the tumescent method using large volumes of dilute lidocaine and epinephrine so that local anesthesia alone could be used.[5]

Neck-specific literature followed. A 1991 study of 500 procedures reported that skin retraction after liposuction differed by treatment site, with the neck favourable;[8] a 2000 series described combining neck liposuction with platysma repair as an alternative to a facelift for cervicomental contouring;[2] and 2010s series documented large-scale safety experience in dermatologic practices.[6][7] Non-surgical competitors appeared in the same period: cryolipolysis was introduced as CoolSculpting in 2010 and later cleared for the submental area,[10] and the FDA approved deoxycholic acid (Kybella) in April 2015 for moderate-to-severe fat below the chin.[9]

sections.h: Who it is used for and how results are described
paras: Papers describe the ideal candidate as someone with localized submental or neck fat and good skin elasticity; skin quality determines how well the neck redrapes after fat removal.[8][3] In a 1991 study, liposuction improved or removed existing skin laxity of the neck, with benefit growing over time, and the author called the neck the site of choice for suction lipectomy; results on the face were more likely to worsen over time.[8]

When the blurred jaw-neck line is due to the shape of the bones rather than fat, Wikipedia notes that deficient jaw projection can make a chin appear to merge with the neck even with little fat, and that chin or jaw surgery may be used for that cause.[15] Surgical reviews likewise stress choosing the correct operation for each patient.[1]

Surgeons note that results depend on skin quality. In the 500-procedure study, restoration of skin condition was tracked at 2 to 3 days and again after at least two months, and the neck showed improved skin laxity over time.[8]

In a 118-patient series of wide-undermining neck liposuction under local anesthesia, the authors reported improvement of neck contour in all patients, redefinition of the cervicomandibular angle and no touch-ups needed.[11] In the 35-patient series that combined liposuction with platysma plication, laser resurfacing and SMAS plication, outcomes were rated good to excellent in 91 percent and fair to good in 9 percent.[2] The corset platysma repair has been revisited as an addition for muscle bands that liposuction alone does not address.[4] These are surgeons' own reports from uncontrolled series.

A review of complications of neck liposuction and submentoplasty states that pitfalls can lead to unfavorable results and that patient selection and choice of operation matter.[1] In a 320-patient series with 8-week follow-up, there were no serious complications; four patients needed closer follow-up for a hematoma, temporary mandibular nerve problems or a throat sensation, and the author noted that neck liposuction needs more monitoring than body liposuction.[6]

A 987-patient series by three dermatologic surgeons reported temporary marginal mandibular nerve dysfunction in 5 patients, submandibular gland ptosis in 1 and arterial bleeding in 1, with no seroma, skin necrosis, scarring or hyperpigmentation reported.[7] Case reports describe Mycobacterium fortuitum infection after neck liposuction[16] and hidradenitis suppurativa of the anterior neck after VASER submental liposuction in a patient with prior gluteal disease.[14]

General liposuction literature lists bleeding, infection, contour irregularities, numbness and rare serious events such as thromboembolism, with risk rising with large volumes and combined surgeries.[5]

Deoxycholic acid (Kybella) is injected into submental fat to break down fat cells, which the body clears over months; it is prescription-only in the US and EU.[9] Cryolipolysis cools fat to reduce it, and has been cleared for submental use; reviews of cryolipolysis report modest measured fat reductions and rare paradoxical adipose hyperplasia (0.12 to 1.0 percent).[10] Chin implants, genioplasty, buccal fat removal and facelift or necklift procedures are other options discussed for the lower face.[13][15]

Human data on neck liposuction are case series and retrospective reviews, such as 987 patients,[7] 320 patients under tumescent anesthesia,[6] 118 patients with wide undermining,[11] 35 patients with platysma repair,[2] and a 500-procedure retraction study.[8] No randomized trial comparing neck liposuction with other submental options was found.

Two registered trials, one testing neck liposuction for obstructive sleep apnea (NCT01117974) and one combining ultrasound with liposuction for skin tightening (NCT01735929), are listed as withdrawn.[17][18] A 12-participant study of deep intervention in the submental region for double chin was registered as completed.[19]

A looksmax.org thread argues that neck liposuction is a very good surgery for people who do not have a severely recessed jaw, and its original poster states that the results are permanent.[20] The 'jawlet' qualifier in the title reflects a common community view that fat removal reveals the jawline only when the underlying jaw is adequate, which echoes surgeons' point about bony causes of a blurred neck line.[20][15] Such posts are individual opinions; published studies do not compare neck liposuction with other options for jaw appearance.
The procedure is grouped with 'hardmaxxing' (surgical) options in these discussions.[20]

lore.intro: Neck liposuction is discussed on looksmax.org as a hardmaxxing option for defining the neck and jaw, usually with the caveat that it suits people whose jawline is held back by fat rather than by bone.[20]

claims.claim: Neck liposuction gives permanent results and suits people who are not 'complete jawlets'.
Removing neck fat reveals a sharper jawline and neck angle.
It will not help if the cause of a weak neck line is a recessed jaw or chin.
The surgery is low-risk and quick because it is done under local anesthesia.
Skin tightens on its own after neck liposuction.
Non-surgical fat removal can do the same job as liposuction.
